claim: At postnatal day 0 (P0), cardiomyocyte myofibrils are already orientated on the longitudinal axis of the cell with the first layer anchored to the plasma membrane through Z-lines.
source: Surprisingly, at P0, while the contractile apparatus is disorganized in the neonatal CM, myofibrils are already orientated on the longitudinal axis of the cell with the first layer already anchored to the plasma membrane through Z-lines, and thus outlining a periodic crest-like architecture, more likely plasma membrane protrusions, which can yet be visualized all along the CM surface (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which provide visual evidence of myofibril orientation and Z-line anchoring at P0.

claim: At P0, no subsarcolemmal mitochondria (SSM) could be observed in cardiomyocytes.
source: At this stage, no SSM could be observed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text following the description of P0 cardiomyocyte structure.

claim: Cardiomyocyte crest maturation occurs in two steps during the postnatal period.
source: Then, crest maturation throughout the postnatal period occurs in two steps.
evidence: The text explicitly describes a two-step maturation process for cardiomyocyte crests.

claim: The first step of crest maturation, completed by P5, relies on the maturation of Z-lines and myofilament alignment.
source: A first early step, already completed by P5, relies on the maturation of the Z-lines, which delimits each sarcomere from the outer myofibril, allowing better visualization of the surface crest structure, concomitant to the myofilament alignment/organization that follows the morphological elongation of the CM (Figure 1A, P5).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations at P5 shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At P5, cardiomyocyte crests still display an unstructured morphology with small heights due to lack or presence of very small SSM.
source: However, crests still display an unstructured morphology and their heights, directly correlated with the SSM number as previously described in adult CMs (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019), are small ('flat'-appearance) due to the lack or the presence of very small SSM, likely immature SSM (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations in Figure 1A and references previous work (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019) establishing the correlation between crest height and SSM number.

claim: Interfibrillar mitochondria (IFM) are much larger but disorganized at P0 and are predominantly located around cardiomyocyte nuclei.
source: By comparison, much larger but disorganized interfibrillar mitochondria (IFM) can be visualized in CMs at birth (P0) predominantly around CM nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), while they mature until P60 through both swelling (completed at P20) and alignment along the myofilaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Interfibrillar mitochondria mature until P60 through both swelling (completed at P20) and alignment along the myofilaments.
source: By comparison, much larger but disorganized interfibrillar mitochondria (IFM) can be visualized in CMs at birth (P0) predominantly around CM nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), while they mature until P60 through both swelling (completed at P20) and alignment along the myofilaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Crest immaturity persists until P20, while the cardiomyocyte has already implemented its rod shape.
source: The crest immaturity persists until P20, a late stage of the postnatal period, while the CM has already implemented its rod shape (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and completed its whole cytoarchitecture (Piquereau et al., 2010), as indicated by the perfect alignment of sarcomere Z-lines between myofibril layers inferred from the α-actinin staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and references previous work (Piquereau et al., 2010).

claim: At P20, cardiomyocytes from left ventricular myocardium display different morphologies with both rod-shaped and spindle-shaped cells, compared to only rod-shaped cells at P60.
source: It is worth noting that at P20, CMs from left ventricular myocardium display different morphologies with both rod-shaped and spindle-shaped CMs when compared with only rod-shaped CMs at P60 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, lower panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, lower panels.

claim: A second maturation step of the surface crests occurs between P20 and P60 through substantial SSM swelling.
source: Interestingly, a second but delayed maturation step of the surface crests occurs between P20 and the adult stage (P60) through substantial SSM swelling (Figure 1A), during which crest heights significantly expand up, correlating with an increase in both the SSM number and area (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations and quantifications shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: Between P20 and P60, crest heights significantly increase, correlating with an increase in both SSM number and area.
source: Interestingly, a second but delayed maturation step of the surface crests occurs between P20 and the adult stage (P60) through substantial SSM swelling (Figure 1A), during which crest heights significantly expand up, correlating with an increase in both the SSM number and area (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Similar P20-P60 crest/SSM maturation was observed in mouse heart tissue.
source: Similar P20-P60 crest/SSM maturation was depicted in the mouse heart tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), thus agreeing with conservation of the postnatal maturation of the heart in mouse and rat as recently reported (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and references recent work (Li et al., 2022).

claim: Claudin-5 protein expression is progressively induced in cardiac tissue at birth (P0), reaching maximal expression at P5-P10.
source: While claudin-5 protein expression is progressively induced in the cardiac tissue at birth (P0), reaching its maximal expression at P5-P10 (Figure 1C, left panel), complete localization of the protein at the lateral membrane of the CM occurs only between P20 and P60 (Figure 1C, right panel), most likely in agreement with the implementation of claudin-5/claudin-5-dependent interactions necessary to clip crests from neighboring CMs that we previously described at the adult stage (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C, left panel.

claim: Complete localization of claudin-5 at the lateral membrane of cardiomyocytes occurs only between P20 and P60.
source: While claudin-5 protein expression is progressively induced in the cardiac tissue at birth (P0), reaching its maximal expression at P5-P10 (Figure 1C, left panel), complete localization of the protein at the lateral membrane of the CM occurs only between P20 and P60 (Figure 1C, right panel), most likely in agreement with the implementation of claudin-5/claudin-5-dependent interactions necessary to clip crests from neighboring CMs that we previously described at the adult stage (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C, right panel, and references previous work (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019).

claim: Atypical tight junctions connecting crests from the lateral face of neighboring cardiomyocytes could be observed only in the P60 adult stage.
source: In line with this mechanism, atypical tight junctions connecting crests from the lateral face of neighbor CMs could be observed only in the P60 adult stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The maturation of the cardiomyocyte lateral surface between P20 and P60 occurs concomitantly with ultimate maturation of both the intercalated disk and the T-tubules.
source: Remarkably, the maturation of the CM lateral surface occurring between P20 and P60, at least in part through the setting of crest–crest interactions, occurs concomitantly with an ultimate maturation of both the ID and the T-tubules, relying on a spatial reorganization of their specific components.
evidence: The text explicitly states this concomitant maturation process.

claim: Connexin 43, desmoplakin 1/2, and N-cadherin are located on both the lateral membrane and the intercalated disk at P20, but fully relocalize to the intercalated disk at P60.
source: Thus, while connexin 43 (gap junctions), desmoplakin 1/2 (desmosomes), and N-cadherin (Adherens junctions) are located on both the lateral membrane and the ID at P20, they fully relocalize to the ID at P60 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: RyR and caveolin-3 (T-tubule markers) are misaligned at P20 while showing perfect alignment along sarcomere Z-lines at P60.
source: Likewise, RyR and caveolin-3, T-tubule markers (see 'Methods'), are still misaligned at P20 while a perfect alignment along the sarcomere Z-lines on the short CM axis can be observed at P60 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A and B.

claim: T-tubule power (regularity) tends to increase after P20 while T-tubule periodicity (frequency) is already established at P20.
source: In agreement, the TT power (TT regularity) tends to increase after P20 while the TT periodicity (frequency) is already established at P20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C and 'Methods').
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8C.

claim: The architecture of the cardiomyocyte plasma membrane as a whole continues to mature late after P20, following the establishment of the rod shape.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the architecture of the CM plasma membrane as a whole still continues to maturate late after P20, following the establishment of the rod shape.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding observations about lateral membrane, intercalated disk, and T-tubule maturation.

claim: Volcano plot analysis and heat map show significant differences between P20 and P60 heart gene expression in mice.
source: Volcano plot analysis of the transcriptome and the heat map clearly show a significant difference between P20 and P60 heart gene expression (Figure 2A and B) with 1000 protein-coding genes that are up- or downregulated between P20 and P60 (p<0.05, fold change ˃ 1.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: 1000 protein-coding genes are up- or downregulated between P20 and P60 in mouse left ventricular tissue (p<0.05, fold change > 1.5).
source: Volcano plot analysis of the transcriptome and the heat map clearly show a significant difference between P20 and P60 heart gene expression (Figure 2A and B) with 1000 protein-coding genes that are up- or downregulated between P20 and P60 (p<0.05, fold change ˃ 1.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analysis revealed upregulated biological pathways between P20 and P60 related to immune defense, muscle cell differentiation, angiogenesis, positive regulation of cell death, different metabolisms including antioxidant defense, plasma membrane-related transport/signaling, and nervous system development.
source: The gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed significantly affected biological pathways (p<0.05) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that are upregulated and mainly related to processes of the immune defense system, muscle cell differentiation, angiogenesis, positive regulation of cell death, different metabolisms including antioxidant defense, plasma membrane-related transport/signaling together with many pathways related to the nervous system development.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many ECM and developmental processes are downregulated between P20 and P60.
source: By contrast, many ECM and developmental processes are downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the context of GO enrichment analysis results.

claim: Some upregulated metabolic pathways between P20 and P60 relate to heart fuels other than fatty acids and glucose (tryptophan, glutamate, glycine/serine/threonine metabolisms), suggesting the heart increases its metabolic flexibility.
source: It is worth noting that some upregulated metabolic pathways relate to heart fuels other than fatty acids and glucose (tryptophan, glutamate, glycine/serine/threonine metabolisms), thus suggesting that the heart increases its metabolic flexibility between P20 and P60.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of upregulated metabolic pathways.

claim: The main downregulation of the transcriptome between P20 and P60 occurs primarily in fibroblast populations and to a lesser extent in cardiomyocyte populations.
source: In line with the GO analysis, we found that the main downregulation of the transcriptome between P20 and P60 occurs primarily in the fibroblast populations known to be involved in the synthesis of the fibrillar ECM but also to a lesser extent in the CM populations (Figure 2D), consistent with the skeletal system and heart development pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The P20-P60 upregulated transcriptome largely refers to ventricular cardiomyocyte populations compared to the downregulated one.
source: By contrast, although all cardiac cells seem to be involved in the transcriptional maturation, the P20-P60 upregulated transcriptome largely referred to the ventricular CM populations compared to the downregulated one (Figure 2D), in agreement with the evidence of a prominent muscle cell differentiation pathway depicted through the GO analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Key cardiomyocyte-specific protein-encoding genes are modulated between P20 and P60, including proteins from the contractile apparatus or regulating the contractile machinery at the lateral membrane.
source: The existence of an important transcriptional maturation step of the CM during the P20-P60 postnatal window is further reinforced by the modulation of key CM-specific protein-encoding genes, especially several proteins from the contractile apparatus or regulating the contractile machinery at the lateral membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The BDH1 gene encoding β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase is remarkably upregulated between P20 and P60.
source: Another CM maturation also occurs at the metabolic level while the metabolic switch of the heart from glycolysis to fatty acid (FA) oxidation was already established during the early postnatal period (Lopaschuk and Jaswal, 2010), with the remarkable upregulation of the BDH1 gene that encodes the β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, the limiting mitochondrial enzyme for ketone body (KB) uptake during fatty acid catabolism, but also to a lesser extent the upregulation of key actors in the glycolytic metabolism (PFKFB2, SLC2A4) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and references previous work (Lopaschuk and Jaswal, 2010).

claim: Key actors in glycolytic metabolism (PFKFB2, SLC2A4) are upregulated to a lesser extent between P20 and P60.
source: Another CM maturation also occurs at the metabolic level while the metabolic switch of the heart from glycolysis to fatty acid (FA) oxidation was already established during the early postnatal period (Lopaschuk and Jaswal, 2010), with the remarkable upregulation of the BDH1 gene that encodes the β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, the limiting mitochondrial enzyme for ketone body (KB) uptake during fatty acid catabolism, but also to a lesser extent the upregulation of key actors in the glycolytic metabolism (PFKFB2, SLC2A4) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Not only the cardiomyocyte but the whole heart continues developing after P20.
source: Overall, these results indicate that not only the CM but the whole heart still continue developing after P20.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the transcriptomic analysis results.

claim: P20 and P60 rats display similar left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF).
source: Longitudinal echocardiographic evaluation reveals a similar left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in both P20 and P60 rats (Figure 3A), indicating earlier maturation of the systolic function during the postnatal period.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Systolic function matures earlier during the postnatal period, before P20.
source: Longitudinal echocardiographic evaluation reveals a similar left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in both P20 and P60 rats (Figure 3A), indicating earlier maturation of the systolic function during the postnatal period.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LVEF is similar at P20 and P60.

claim: Specific changes in diastolic function occur between P20 and P60 rats, including significant increase in passive filling (E/A) and improvement in relaxation (decrease in IVRT, increase in e'/a' and e', without change in E/e').
source: By contrast, we observed specific changes in the diastolic function between P20 and P60 as measured by noninvasive Doppler imaging and showing a significant increase in passive filling (E/A) and an improvement in relaxation (decrease in the isovolumic relaxation time [IVRT], increase in the e'/a' and the early diastolic mitral annular tissue velocity e', without change in the LV filling pressures E/e') (Figure 3A), most likely indicating that the diastolic function of the rat heart maturates during the late postnatal period, between P20 and P60.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The diastolic function of the rat heart matures during the late postnatal period, between P20 and P60.
source: By contrast, we observed specific changes in the diastolic function between P20 and P60 as measured by noninvasive Doppler imaging and showing a significant increase in passive filling (E/A) and an improvement in relaxation (decrease in the isovolumic relaxation time [IVRT], increase in the e'/a' and the early diastolic mitral annular tissue velocity e', without change in the LV filling pressures E/e') (Figure 3A), most likely indicating that the diastolic function of the rat heart maturates during the late postnatal period, between P20 and P60.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in diastolic parameters between P20 and P60.

claim: P20 and P60 rats display similar heart rates.
source: Further confirming the P20-P60 set-up of the adult diastolic function, while P20 and P60 rats display similar heart rates, invasive left ventricle catheter analysis shows increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) as well as end-diastolic pressure (EDP) and an improvement in diastolic relaxation reflected by the dP/dtmin and the decreased time constant of isovolumic relaxation (Tau) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cardiac catheterization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Between P20 and P60, rats show increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) as well as end-diastolic pressure (EDP).
source: Further confirming the P20-P60 set-up of the adult diastolic function, while P20 and P60 rats display similar heart rates, invasive left ventricle catheter analysis shows increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) as well as end-diastolic pressure (EDP) and an improvement in diastolic relaxation reflected by the dP/dtmin and the decreased time constant of isovolumic relaxation (Tau) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cardiac catheterization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Between P20 and P60, rats show improvement in diastolic relaxation reflected by dP/dtmin and decreased time constant of isovolumic relaxation (Tau).
source: Further confirming the P20-P60 set-up of the adult diastolic function, while P20 and P60 rats display similar heart rates, invasive left ventricle catheter analysis shows increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) as well as end-diastolic pressure (EDP) and an improvement in diastolic relaxation reflected by the dP/dtmin and the decreased time constant of isovolumic relaxation (Tau) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cardiac catheterization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The late P20-P60 developmental stage of the heart is specifically required for the maturation of the diastolic function.
source: These data indicate that the late P20-P60 developmental stage of the heart is specifically required for the maturation of the diastolic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the functional data from echocardiography and catheterization.

claim: Cardiomyocytes from the left ventricle of rat hearts undergo significant hypertrophy between P20 and P60 as indicated by substantial increase in cross-sectional area.
source: We observed that CMs from the left ventricle of rat hearts undergo significant hypertrophy between P20 and P60 as indicated by the substantial increase in their cross-sectional area (Figure 4A), which peaks at P45 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and in both their long and short axes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area peaks at P45 during the P20-P60 period.
source: We observed that CMs from the left ventricle of rat hearts undergo significant hypertrophy between P20 and P60 as indicated by the substantial increase in their cross-sectional area (Figure 4A), which peaks at P45 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and in both their long and short axes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Between P20 and P60, cardiomyocytes increase in both their long and short axes.
source: We observed that CMs from the left ventricle of rat hearts undergo significant hypertrophy between P20 and P60 as indicated by the substantial increase in their cross-sectional area (Figure 4A), which peaks at P45 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and in both their long and short axes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar late hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes was observed in mice between P20 and P60.
source: Similar late hypertrophy of CMs was observed in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: P20-P60 cardiomyocyte hypertrophy was confirmed by echocardiography showing significant increase in left ventricle posterior wall thickening (LVPWd) and cavity size (LVEDV, LVEDD).
source: This P20-P60 CM hypertrophy was confirmed by echocardiography with a significant increase in the left ventricle posterior wall thickening (LVPWd) and cavity size (LVEDV, LVEDD) (Figure 4C), all indicative of an overall heart growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: P20-P60 physiological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy is atypical since it is not correlated with an increase in the myofilament compartment, as indicated by constant myofibril number.
source: Surprisingly, this physiological CM hypertrophy is atypical since it is not correlated with an expected increase in the myofilament compartment as indicated by the constant number of CM myofibrils between P20 and P60 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The heart weight to body weight ratio decreases between P20 and P60.
source: This is corroborated by a marked decrease in the heart weight to body weight ratio during this period (Figure 4E), as previously reported (Piquereau et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E and references previous work (Piquereau et al., 2010).

claim: Between P20 and P60, there is a significant and specific increase in sarcomere heights with no variation of sarcomere lengths.
source: Interestingly, we also noticed a significant and specific increase in the sarcomere heights with no variation of the sarcomere lengths (Figure 4F) which was inversely correlated with a decrease in the inter-lateral space between two CMs (Figure 4G), likely indicative of a lateral stretch of the CMs and a cardiac tissue compaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The increase in sarcomere heights between P20 and P60 is inversely correlated with a decrease in the inter-lateral space between two cardiomyocytes.
source: Interestingly, we also noticed a significant and specific increase in the sarcomere heights with no variation of the sarcomere lengths (Figure 4F) which was inversely correlated with a decrease in the inter-lateral space between two CMs (Figure 4G), likely indicative of a lateral stretch of the CMs and a cardiac tissue compaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4G.

claim: The changes in sarcomere height and inter-lateral space are indicative of lateral stretch of cardiomyocytes and cardiac tissue compaction.
source: Interestingly, we also noticed a significant and specific increase in the sarcomere heights with no variation of the sarcomere lengths (Figure 4F) which was inversely correlated with a decrease in the inter-lateral space between two CMs (Figure 4G), likely indicative of a lateral stretch of the CMs and a cardiac tissue compaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in sarcomere height and inter-lateral space.

claim: Larger distances between thick myosin filaments are observed at P60 than at P20.
source: Further supporting the CM lateral stretch that should distend the myofibrils, we observed larger distances between the thick myosin filaments at P60 than at P20 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ephrin-B1 reaches maximal expression very early during the postnatal period (P5).
source: As shown in Figure 5A and similarly to what we observed for claudin-5, ephrin-B1 reaches maximal expression very early during the postnatal period (P5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Complete trafficking of ephrin-B1 from the cytosol to the cardiomyocyte surface is only achieved at P60.
source: However, the complete trafficking of ephrin-B1 from the cytosol to the CM surface is only achieved at P60.
evidence: This is stated in the context of describing ephrin-B1 expression and localization during postnatal development.

claim: Ephrin-B1 does not contribute to major cardiac developmental processes before P20, as P20 CM-specific Efnb1 KO and WT mice demonstrate almost similar left ventricular transcriptome.
source: It is worth noting that ephrin-B1 does not contribute to major cardiac developmental processes before P20 since P20 CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice and WT mice demonstrate almost similar left ventricular transcriptome as highlighted by the volcano plot (only six genes different between the two genotypes) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lack of ephrin-B1 in cardiomyocytes partially impairs the P20-P60 physiological hypertrophy.
source: At the cellular level, the lack of ephrin-B1 in the CM partially impairs the P20-P60 physiological hypertrophy of the CM (Figure 5B), without modification of the myofibril number (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Efnb1 deletion does not modify myofibril number in cardiomyocytes.
source: At the cellular level, the lack of ephrin-B1 in the CM partially impairs the P20-P60 physiological hypertrophy of the CM (Figure 5B), without modification of the myofibril number (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Efnb1 deletion more specifically impedes the lateral stretch (short axis) of cardiomyocytes but not the longitudinal one.
source: Consistent with ephrin-B1-specific expression at the lateral membrane, Efnb1 deletion more specifically impedes the lateral stretch (short axis) of the CM but not the longitudinal one (Figure 5D) and accordingly leads to a decrease in both the sarcomere heights (Figure 5F) and the tissue compaction (increased lateral interspace) (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Efnb1 deletion leads to a decrease in sarcomere heights.
source: Consistent with ephrin-B1-specific expression at the lateral membrane, Efnb1 deletion more specifically impedes the lateral stretch (short axis) of the CM but not the longitudinal one (Figure 5D) and accordingly leads to a decrease in both the sarcomere heights (Figure 5F) and the tissue compaction (increased lateral interspace) (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Efnb1 deletion leads to decreased tissue compaction (increased lateral interspace between cardiomyocytes).
source: Consistent with ephrin-B1-specific expression at the lateral membrane, Efnb1 deletion more specifically impedes the lateral stretch (short axis) of the CM but not the longitudinal one (Figure 5D) and accordingly leads to a decrease in both the sarcomere heights (Figure 5F) and the tissue compaction (increased lateral interspace) (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: P20 CM-specific Efnb1 KO and WT mice harbor similar unstructured surface crests with immature SSM, but only WT mice undergo crest maturation at P60.
source: At the lateral membrane level, P20 CM-specific Efnb1 KO and WT mice harbor similar unstructured surface crests with immature SSM but only WT mice underwent crest maturation at P60 (Figure 5E), thus demonstrating a key role for ephrin-B1 in the postnatal maturation of the surface crest/SSM.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations and quantifications shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ephrin-B1 plays a key role in the postnatal maturation of the surface crest/SSM.
source: At the lateral membrane level, P20 CM-specific Efnb1 KO and WT mice harbor similar unstructured surface crests with immature SSM but only WT mice underwent crest maturation at P60 (Figure 5E), thus demonstrating a key role for ephrin-B1 in the postnatal maturation of the surface crest/SSM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that crest maturation occurs only in WT mice and not in Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: 2-month-old CM-specific Efnb1 KO and WT mice display similar heart rate and LVEF.
source: As previously reported (Genet et al., 2012), we did not notice differences in heart rate and LVEF between 2-month-old WT and CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 6A and references previous work (Genet et al., 2012).

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display a significant decrease in LVPWd and an increase in left ventricular internal diameter (LVIDd) and volume (LVEDV).
source: However, and consistent with the role of ephrin-B1 in the lateral stretch-based hypertrophy of the CM, CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display a significant decrease in LVPWd conversely to an increase in left ventricular internal diameter (left ventricular internal diameter end diastole [LVIDd]) and volume (LV end-diastolic volume [LVEDV]) (Figure 6A), in agreement with our previous study (Genet et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 6A and references previous work (Genet et al., 2012).

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display significantly elongated IVRT, increased left atrial volume (LA/Ao), and decreased E/A as well as heterogeneous E/E', indicative of impaired LV relaxation.
source: More interestingly, compared with WT mice, CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display significantly elongated IVRT, increased left atrial volume (left atrial to aortic root ratio [LA/Ao]), and decreased E/A as well as heterogeneous E/E' (Figure 6A), all indicative of impaired LV relaxation.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice show a significant decrease in ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS), reflecting abnormal longitudinal systolic function.
source: Despite preservation of the LVEF, we also measured a significant decrease in ventricular global longitudinal strain (LV-GLS) in KO mice (Figure 6A) reflecting abnormal longitudinal systolic function.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 2-month-old CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice exhibit increased EDP and heterogeneous dP/dt but similar relaxation time constants (tau) compared with age-matched WT mice.
source: Diastolic dysfunction in KO mice was further confirmed by cardiac catheterization since 2-month-old CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice exhibit increased EDP and heterogeneous dP/dt but with similar relaxation time constants (tau) compared with age-matched WT mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cardiac catheterization data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The diastolic defects of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice rely on a specific impairment of cardiomyocyte relaxation, with significantly reduced diastolic basal sarcomere length shortening and relaxation velocities in isolated intact cardiomyocytes.
source: The diastolic defects of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice rely on a specific impairment of the CM relaxation since both the diastolic basal sarcomere length (SL) shortening and relaxation velocities are significantly reduced in isolated intact CMs from CM-specific Efnb1 KO compared to WT mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sarcomere length measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The auxotonic contraction indexed by sarcomere length shortening and shortening velocities are significantly decreased in cardiomyocytes from CM-specific Efnb1 KO compared to WT cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) phenotype in which CM contraction defects coexist with the relaxation impairment (Methawasin et al., 2016; Primessnig et al., 2016; Schiattarella et al., 2019), the auxotonic contraction indexed by the SL shortening as well as the SL shortening velocities are also significantly decreased in CMs from CM-specific Efnb1 KO compared to WT CMs (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sarcomere length measurements shown in Figure 6C and references previous work (Methawasin et al., 2016; Primessnig et al., 2016; Schiattarella et al., 2019).

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display significant exercise intolerance compared with WT mice, as indicated by significant decrease in maximum oxygen uptake.
source: Finally, CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice also display significant exercise intolerance compared with WT mice, as indicated by the significant decrease in maximum oxygen uptake (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by exercise tolerance data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Young adult male CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice recapitulate some features of clinical HFpEF.
source: Together, these results indicate that young adult male CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice recapitulate some features of clinical HFpEF, thus demonstrating a pivotal role for ephrin-B1 in the control of the diastolic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the functional characterization of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: Ephrin-B1 plays a pivotal role in the control of the diastolic function.
source: Together, these results indicate that young adult male CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice recapitulate some features of clinical HFpEF, thus demonstrating a pivotal role for ephrin-B1 in the control of the diastolic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice exhibit diastolic dysfunction.

claim: A recent RNAseq study on ventricles from HFpEF, HFrEF, and control patients reported specific and more significant downregulation of the Efnb1 gene in HFpEF than HFrEF patients.
source: In line with this assumption, a recent RNAseq study performed on ventricles from HFpEF, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and control patients reported a specific and more significant downregulation of the Efnb1 gene in HFpEF than HFrEF patients (p=9.10–14 HFpEF vs. control, p=2.10–5 HFrEF vs. control, p=0.005 HFpEF versus HFrEF) (Hahn et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citing a recent RNAseq study (Hahn et al., 2021).

claim: Injection of tamoxifen for four consecutive days in 2-month-old Efnb1flox/flox-αMHC-Cre+ mice led to a specific but partial deletion (~50%) of ephrin-B1 in cardiomyocytes after 1 month following the last tamoxifen treatment.
source: In agreement with most conditional mouse models, injection of tamoxifen for four consecutive days in 2-month-old Efnb1flox/flox-αMHC-Cre+ (cKO) and their Efnb1flox/flox-αMHC-Cre- littermates (Ctrl) led to a specific but partial deletion (~50 %) of ephrin-B1 in CMs from the cKO mice only when analyzed after 1 month following the last tamoxifen treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Efnb1 at the adult stage led to partial loss of cardiomyocyte surface crests in cKO mice compared to control littermates.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, deletion of Efnb1 at the adult stage led to partial loss of the CM surface crests in cKO mice compared to their control littermates.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations and quantifications shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Efnb1 cKO mice display significant left ventricle dilatation as reflected by increase in LVIDd associated with a trend to increase in LVEDV, lack of left ventricle hypertrophy (IVSd, LVPWd), and preserved ejection fraction (LVEF).
source: Likewise Efnb1 KO mice, cKO mice display a significant left ventricle dilatation as reflected by the increase in the left ventricular internal diameter (LVIDd) associated with a trend to the increase in the left ventricle volume (LVEDV), a lack of left ventricle hypertrophy (IVSd, LVPWd), and a preserved ejection fraction (LVEF) (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Deletion of Efnb1 at adulthood promotes significant diastolic defects, with cKO mice showing significantly elongated IVRT with no modification of E/A, significant increase in EDP, heterogeneous dP/dt but similar relaxation time constants compared with control littermates.
source: More interestingly, the deletion of Efnb1 at the adulthood still promotes significant diastolic defects since cKO mice show significant elongated IVRT with no modification of the E/A together with a significant increase in EDP, heterogeneous dP/dt but similar relaxation time constants compared with their control littermates (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic and catheterization data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Ephrin-B1 controls the maturation of cardiomyocyte surface crests during the P20-P60 postnatal period and contributes to the regulation of the adult diastolic function.
source: Altogether, these results clearly demonstrate that ephrin-B1 controls the maturation of the CM surface crests during the P20-P60 postnatal period and contributes to the regulation of the adult diastolic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the results from both constitutive and conditional Efnb1 knockout mice.

claim: While young adult (2 months) CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display LV diastolic dysfunction with preserved ejection fraction, LVEF decreased progressively over time, starting to develop moderate HFrEF at 9 months and evolving toward severe HFrEF by 13 months.
source: Interestingly, while in young adulthood (2 months) CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display LV diastolic dysfunction with preserved ejection fraction compared to WT mice, LVEF decreased progressively over time in these mice, which start developing moderate HFrEF at 9 months, evolving toward severe HFrEF by 13 months (Figure 8A) and 100% mortality after 15 months (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal echocardiographic data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 100% of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice died after 15 months.
source: Interestingly, while in young adulthood (2 months) CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice display LV diastolic dysfunction with preserved ejection fraction compared to WT mice, LVEF decreased progressively over time in these mice, which start developing moderate HFrEF at 9 months, evolving toward severe HFrEF by 13 months (Figure 8A) and 100% mortality after 15 months (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: LVIDd and LVEDV significantly increase over time only in CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.
source: Accordingly, LVIDd and LVEDV significantly increase over time only in KO mice (Figure 8A) concurrently with the development of compensatory cardiac hypertrophy (IVSd, Figure 8A, C and D) and fibrosis around 12 months of age (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal echocardiographic data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice develop compensatory cardiac hypertrophy (IVSd) concurrently with the progression of heart failure.
source: Accordingly, LVIDd and LVEDV significantly increase over time only in KO mice (Figure 8A) concurrently with the development of compensatory cardiac hypertrophy (IVSd, Figure 8A, C and D) and fibrosis around 12 months of age (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiographic data and heart weight measurements shown in Figure 8A, C, and D.

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice develop cardiac fibrosis around 12 months of age.
source: Accordingly, LVIDd and LVEDV significantly increase over time only in KO mice (Figure 8A) concurrently with the development of compensatory cardiac hypertrophy (IVSd, Figure 8A, C and D) and fibrosis around 12 months of age (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fibrosis quantification shown in Figure 8E.

claim: T-tubule misalignment from Z-lines is already detectable but limited to discrete local regions in some KO cardiomyocytes at 2 months of age, and this disorganization progressively spreads over time to all cardiomyocytes after 12 months.
source: Corroborating the HF progression in CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice, while T-tubule misalignment from Z-lines (HFrEF marker) is already detectable but limited to discrete local regions in the cardiac tissue of some KO CMs at 2 months of age, this disorganization progressively spreads over time to all CMs after 12 months compared with WT mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Lack of ephrin-B1 in cardiomyocytes primarily impairs the diastolic function of young adult mice, which progressively switches toward a systolic defect with aging.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the lack of ephrin-B1 in CM primarily impairs the diastolic function of young adult mice, which progressively switch toward a systolic defect with aging.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the longitudinal functional characterization of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: Specific defects in the maturation of cardiomyocyte surface crests during late postnatal development will early impact the diastolic function of adults, which will be revealed later in life through the onset of systolic dysfunction.
source: Hence, specific defects in the maturation of the CM surface crests during the late postnatal development that will early impact the diastolic function of the adults, more likely asymptomatic in young adulthood, will be only revealed later in life through the onset of the systolic dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the progressive phenotype observed in CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: A new developmental stage occurs in the late postnatal period between P20 and P60, during which crests of the cardiomyocyte lateral membrane mature through SSM biogenesis, swelling, and crest-crest interactions within the tissue through an ephrin-B1/claudin-5 mechanism.
source: In this study, we describe a new developmental stage occurring in the late postnatal period between P20 and P60, during which crests of the CM lateral membrane maturate through SSM biogenesis, swelling, and crest–crest interactions within the tissue through an ephrin-B1/claudin-5 mechanism, thus allowing CM lateral stretching and a global compaction of the cardiac tissue (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The P20-P60 maturation mechanism allows cardiomyocyte lateral stretching and global compaction of the cardiac tissue.
source: In this study, we describe a new developmental stage occurring in the late postnatal period between P20 and P60, during which crests of the CM lateral membrane maturate through SSM biogenesis, swelling, and crest–crest interactions within the tissue through an ephrin-B1/claudin-5 mechanism, thus allowing CM lateral stretching and a global compaction of the cardiac tissue (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the crest maturation mechanism.

claim: The P20-P60 maturation mechanism regulates the adult diastolic function.
source: We demonstrate that this mechanism regulates the adult diastolic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the functional findings of the study.

claim: Ephrin-B1 controls the architecture of the lateral membrane and the overall adult rod shape of cardiomyocytes.
source: We previously demonstrated that ephrin-B1 controls the architecture of the lateral membrane and the overall adult rod shape of the CM (Genet et al., 2012).
evidence: This references previous work by the authors (Genet et al., 2012).

claim: Ephrin-B1 controls the maturity of the crest/SSM architectural motif at the lateral membrane.
source: Here, we now further demonstrated that ephrin-B1 controls the maturity of the crest/SSM architectural motif at the lateral membrane, thus playing a key role in the adult crest–crest interactions between neighboring CMs and in overall tissue cohesion.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the current study.

claim: Lateral cardiomyocyte interactions likely dictate a mechanical lateral stretch of the cardiomyocyte, allowing perfect stacking between myofibril layers.
source: These lateral CM interactions likely dictate a mechanical lateral stretch of the CM, allowing perfect stacking between myofibril layers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of ephrin-B1 on crest-crest interactions and CM morphology.

claim: Crest-crest interactions might contribute to controlling the relaxation length of the sarcomere.
source: Consequently, crest–crest interactions might contribute to controlling the relaxation length of the sarcomere, a mechanism that we previously suggested to be dependent on crest height (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on previous work (Guilbeau-Frugier et al., 2019) and current findings.

claim: The ephrin-B1-dependent lateral stretch of cardiomyocytes is necessary for the spatial arrangement of T-tubules during P20-P60 development.
source: This ephrin-B1-dependent lateral stretch of the CM is also necessary for the spatial arrangement of the T-tubules and most likely its ensuing function during the P20-P60 development, as supported by the T-tubule disorganization in the CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of T-tubule disorganization in CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: By altering T-tubule structure, lack of ephrin-B1 could influence Ca2+ entry/Ca2+ exit.
source: Thus, by altering the T-tubule structure, lack of ephrin-B1 could influence the Ca2+ entry/Ca2+ exit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known role of T-tubules in Ca2+ handling.

claim: T-tubule disorganization in cardiomyocytes of Efnb1CM-/- KO mice is progressive, with mild disorganization correlating with diastolic dysfunction only, while extensive disorganization is observed in HFrEF.
source: It is worth noting that T-tubule disorganization in the CMs of Efnb1CM-/- KO mice is progressive with mild disorganization correlating with diastolic dysfunction only, while extensive disorganization is observed in HFrEF.
evidence: This is based on the longitudinal observations of T-tubule organization in CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: Defects in T-tubule architecture/function are a hallmark of HFrEF.
source: Although defects in T-tubule architecture/function are a hallmark of HFrEF (Guo et al., 2013), it has been poorly examined in HFpEF, only one recent study reported that this mechanism is etiology-dependent (Frisk et al., 2021).
evidence: This references previous work (Guo et al., 2013; Frisk et al., 2021).

claim: CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice exhibit a progressive cardiac phenotype starting from primarily diastolic defect that progressively switches toward mild and then severe HFrEF and finally to death.
source: An exciting feature of the CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice is the progressive cardiac phenotype starting from a primarily diastolic defect that progressively switches toward a mild and then severe HFrEF and finally to death, thus highlighting the substantial cardioprotective role of the surface crests/SSM of the lateral membrane.
evidence: This is a summary of the longitudinal phenotypic characterization of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice.

claim: The progressive phenotype of CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice highlights the substantial cardioprotective role of the surface crests/SSM of the lateral membrane.
source: An exciting feature of the CM-specific Efnb1 KO mice is the progressive cardiac phenotype starting from a primarily diastolic defect that progressively switches toward a mild and then severe HFrEF and finally to death, thus highlighting the substantial cardioprotective role of the surface crests/SSM of the lateral membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the severe consequences of losing ephrin-B1 and crest maturation.
